newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. deplores Iraqi refusal over missile engines.
newsitem.headline: U.N. deplores Iraqi refusal over missile engines.

text.p: The United Nations Security Council Monday deplored Iraq's refusal to allow some 130 missile engines to be taken abroad for examination by experts and reminded Baghdad of its obligation to comply with Gulf war disarmament resolutions.

A statement read out at a formal council meeting was a followup to an oral report earlier this month by chief U.N. weapons inspector Rolf Ekeus that he had again been unable to secure permission to remove SCUD missile engines and other components which Iraq destroyed and buried without U.N. supervision shortly after the 1991 war.

When Ekeus reported to the council December 18 he said he believed Iraq still had "a significant number of operational missiles which could constitute a complete missile force," but gave no specific number.
He said the question of removing missile engines would again be dealt with when he next met Iraqi deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz some time in February.

The council issued its statement the day before it was due to conduct a 60-day review of sanctions imposed on Iraq since its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait. The sanctions are certain to remain unchanged, as they have been since they were first enacted.

A prime condition of an easing of the sanctions is a report to the council by the special commission that Iraq has fulfilled all obligations calling for the scrapping of its nuclear, chemical, biological and ballistic missile potential.

Monday's council statement has no effect on an "oil-for-food" deal which went into force earlier this monmth permitting Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian supplies to help offset the effects of sanctions on Iraqi civilians.

The U.N. special commission (UNSCOM) in charge of scrapping Iraq's weapons of mass destruction had first tried to take the missile parts out of the country in November to obtain a definitive accounting of any remaining stocks.

The statement read out by council President Paolo Fulci of Italy said the council "deplores the refusal by Iraq to allow the special commission to remove approximately 130 missile engines from Iraq for analysis by a team of international experts under the special commission."

Calling for a full accounting of Iraq's missiles with a range greater than 150 kilometres (94 miles), the council reminded Iraq of "its obligation to comply with the provisions of the relevant resolutions and the need to cooperate fully with the special commission."
"In this perspective, the council affirms that Iraq is required to allow the special commission to remove the missile engines from its territory," the statement said.
